channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Spotify Plans to Charge $4 to $5 Extra for an AI Remix Service, the FT Reports
item.description: The service, reported to be planned for the first quarter of 2027, would let subscribers remake songs with AI — a folk track as a dance track, or one artist covering another. Spotify has licensing deals with Universal, Merlin and Believe, and is still negotiating with Sony and Warner, the FT reported via Reuters.
item.content:encoded:
Spotify plans to launch an AI music remix service in the first quarter of 2027, the Financial Times reported on Friday, in a report carried by Reuters. The service would let subscribers use AI to make their own versions of songs — turning a folk song into a dance track, or making one artist appear to cover another's song — for an additional $4 to $5 a month, according to the report. Spotify did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment, and the timing is reported to target an unveiling around the Grammy Awards in February.

The licensing is the substance of the story. The FT reported that Spotify has reached deals with Universal Music Group, the independent label group Merlin and the French company Believe, and is still negotiating with Sony Music and Warner Music. A remix feature built on licensed catalogues is a different product from the unlicensed AI covers that have circulated online for two years: the labels are being paid before the feature exists, and the two largest remaining catalogues are the price of completing it. Whether listeners will pay a second monthly fee, on top of a subscription, to remake songs they already stream is the consumer question the 2027 launch will answer.

item.title: Samsung's Operating Profit Hit a Record 107.4 Trillion Won, Almost All of It From Chips
item.description: Samsung confirmed third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, the first quarter above 100 trillion won for any technology company. Its chip division earned 106.5 trillion won of it; the division that makes its phones and appliances lost money for a second straight quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Samsung Electronics confirmed its full third-quarter results on Thursday in Seoul. Revenue was 195.25 trillion won and operating profit was 107.44 trillion won — about $80 billion — up roughly ninefold from a year earlier and 20% from the second quarter. Samsung is the first technology company to report operating profit above 100 trillion won in a single quarter. Both figures matched the preliminary guidance the company issued on October 8; the new information in Thursday's report is the division breakdown and the outlook given on the earnings call.

The Device Solutions division — memory, chip design and foundry — earned 106.5 trillion won of operating profit on 147.1 trillion won of revenue, about 99% of the company's total. Memory revenue was 140.7 trillion won, up 427% year over year. Samsung said sales of HBM4, its newest high-bandwidth memory, more than tripled from the second quarter and made up 60% of its HBM sales, and that average DRAM selling prices rose about 20% in the quarter. Jaejune Kim, the executive vice president for memory sales and marketing, told analysts that Samsung's 2027 HBM supply is already sold out. The Device eXperience division — phones, televisions and appliances — posted an operating loss of 800 billion won, its second consecutive quarterly loss, as the memory prices that enrich the chip division raise its own component costs.

Samsung approved a third-quarter dividend of 30 trillion won and said full-year capital spending will be about 84.4 trillion won, most of it in the chip division. It expects AI-related memory demand to grow faster than supply in 2027. Samsung shares fell 5.48% in Seoul on Thursday despite the record result. The division split is the week's supplier story in one company: the same memory shortage is a record profit on one side of Samsung and a loss on the other.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Opentrons Raised $40 Million to Put AI-Driven Laboratory Robots in More Labs
item.description: Opentrons builds open, programmable robots that run laboratory experiments, and says more than 11,000 of them are deployed in over 80 countries. The $40 million Series E, led by Avego, funds the software and data layer that lets AI systems design, run and revise experiments in a continuous loop.
item.content:encoded:
Opentrons Labworks announced a $40 million Series E financing on Thursday, led by the healthcare investor Avego with participation from BroadOak Capital Partners. Existing investors include SoftBank Vision Fund and Khosla Ventures. The company, founded in 2014 and based in Long Island City, New York, is led by chief executive James Atwood. It did not disclose a valuation.

Opentrons builds laboratory robots — the Flex platform — that are open and programmable through an API, so experiments can be specified in software, run by the robot, and repeated identically in another laboratory. The company says more than 11,000 of its robots are deployed in laboratories in over 80 countries, including at 90% of the top 20 global pharmaceutical companies and every top-15 US research university. Those deployment figures are the company's. The new capital goes to scaling its robotics, software and data infrastructure, to AI-driven experimental execution, and to expansion into new markets.

The company's stated problem is a sequencing gap in AI-driven science: frontier models can now generate hypotheses and design experiments faster than physical laboratories can run them, so the bottleneck moves from the model to the bench. Opentrons' answer is to make the bench programmable — each experiment run on its robots produces structured, reproducible data that the next round of model work can use. The round lands in a competitive stretch for laboratory automation: the British company Automata raised $45 million in February, and Multiply Labs raised $75 million this month for robotic biomanufacturing (Dealroom). What distinguishes the claims here is installed base: Opentrons is selling an execution layer on top of 11,000 machines already in laboratories, not asking laboratories to adopt a first machine.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Microsoft Booked $10 Billion in Revenue From OpenAI in One Quarter, Its Filing Shows
item.description: Microsoft's quarterly filing discloses $10.0 billion of revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI in the three months to September 30 — nearly 11% of its total revenue — and $7.2 billion of receivables from OpenAI at quarter-end, up from $6.0 billion in June.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's Form 10-Q, filed this week, discloses $10.0 billion of revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI in the three months ended September 30, including revenue-sharing payments (TechCrunch, reading the filing). The figure is nearly 11% of Microsoft's $92.3 billion of quarterly revenue (Edition 011). Revenue from OpenAI for the full fiscal year to June 2026 was $24.1 billion. Microsoft did not break the $10 billion down between Azure cloud services and revenue sharing.

The same filing puts accounts receivable from OpenAI at $7.2 billion on September 30, up from $6.0 billion on June 30. Receivables are amounts owed for past transactions; they are not additional revenue, and the filing does not say why the balance grew. Microsoft holds an approximately 24% interest in OpenAI on an as-converted basis, down from about 25% in June, and reports $13.0 billion of funding commitments to OpenAI, of which $12.0 billion had been funded by September 30.

The disclosure matters because of where it sits. The $10 billion appears in the quarterly filing's related-party notes, not in the earnings release that carried the quarter's headlines. One customer — a company Microsoft part-owns, funds, and supplies — now accounts for about a ninth of its revenue, and the document that establishes the figure is the filing, read after the earnings call. OpenAI's bridge signatures are due today; what its largest partner's books show is part of the evidence those signatures are written against.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Intel Beat Third-Quarter Estimates, Then Guided the Fourth Quarter Well Below Them
item.description: Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion and adjusted earnings of 52 cents a share beat the 40 cents expected, with data-center and AI revenue up 78%. The fourth-quarter guide — revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion against $17.1 billion expected — sent the shares down sharply after hours.
item.content:encoded:
Intel reported third-quarter results after Thursday's close. Revenue rose 21% year over year to $16.51 billion, in line with the $16.5 billion consensus compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings were 52 cents a share, against 40 cents expected, and adjusted gross margin was 44.1%, above the company's 42% guidance. Intel said it was the eighth consecutive quarter in which revenue, gross margin and earnings beat its own guidance. Data Center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 billion. Client Computing and Physical AI revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion; Intel attributed the weakness to industry-wide memory shortages raising PC component prices and to limited customer IT budgets.

The fourth-quarter guidance reversed the response. Intel forecast revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion and adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share, against analyst expectations of about $17.1 billion and 43 cents, with adjusted gross margin of 38%. Shares fell more than 16% in extended trading; some market reports put the after-hours decline near 23%. Intel said total capital spending for 2026 will remain about $20 billion and rise significantly in 2027 to expand manufacturing capacity for AI server CPUs. Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said 2027 will be an investment year in which the company may not achieve positive free cash flow.

Intel's quarter is the supplier side of this week's results read from the other end. The memory makers — SK Hynix (Edition 011) and Samsung, in this edition — reported record margins because memory is scarce. Intel's client business is one of the buyers paying for that scarcity, in a quarter when its data-center business grew at its fastest rate in 15 years on the same AI demand.

item.title: Google's AI Search Would Not Say Who Won the 2020 Election
item.description: Asked who won the 2020 US presidential election, Google's AI Mode pointed users to Federal Election Commission reports instead of answering. It answered correctly for 2016 and 2024. Google called it a technical gap and said on Thursday the 2020 responses were fixed, six days before the midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Google's AI Mode would not say who won the 2020 US presidential election. USA Today reported that on Wednesday, asked the question directly, the AI search feature answered with a pointer to certified Federal Election Commission reports rather than a name. Asked about 2016 and 2024, it answered Donald Trump correctly. The issue appeared only in AI Mode, not in the Gemini app. Google said on X that a technical gap in how its systems verify election responses affected 2020 results — and, it said, 2022 Senate races — and posted on Thursday that the 2020 responses were fixed.

The timing is the story's weight: the failure surfaced six days before the November 3 midterm elections. OpenAI is running an election operation to monitor model behavior and will carry Associated Press vote counts on election night, according to its October posts. Anthropic says Claude draws official voting information from Democracy Works, the nonpartisan civic technology organization, and displays a banner linking to its tools. Four congressional Democrats wrote to the large AI companies on October 20 saying some chatbots' error rates on election and voting questions were unacceptably high. A search feature that declines to state a certified result is not misinformation; it is an absence where the product's purpose is an answer, five days before an election in which its safeguards are the companies' own argument for being trusted with the count.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The Earnings Are In. The Financing Question Remains.
item.description: Four earnings reports and a Federal Reserve decision closed the week this paper set as the buildout's hearing. Demand passed every test put to it: the three largest cloud businesses grew 39% to 103%. The disagreement that remains is narrower — who carries the cost while the returns arrive, and at what interest rate.
item.content:encoded:
The hearing is over. Between Wednesday and Thursday night, the Federal Reserve decided, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon reported — the calendar this paper set in Edition 007 as the buildout's first full examination. Meta reported earlier in the month. The results agree on the point the spending's defenders needed: demand is not the weak part of the account. Azure revenue grew 48% and was disclosed in dollars for the first time. Google Cloud revenue grew 103%. AWS revenue grew 39%, its fastest rate in nearly five years, to a $184 billion annualized rate. Amazon's operating income rose 61% to a record margin.

The suppliers gave the same testimony from the other side of the invoice. SK Hynix reported an operating margin of 79.7% and contracts covering more than half of its 2027 and 2028 production (Edition 011). Samsung's chip division earned 99% of a record 107.4 trillion won operating profit, and its 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply is already sold out. Intel is the exception that locates the rule: its data-center revenue grew 78%, but its client business shrank under the memory prices the other suppliers are charging, and its shares fell on a fourth-quarter guide that assumes the squeeze continues.

What the week did not settle is the financing. The three cloud reports carried three different cash outcomes: free cash flow of positive $18.6 billion at Microsoft, negative $9.1 billion in Alphabet's quarter, and negative $42.4 billion over Amazon's last 12 months. Alphabet has raised $147.2 billion from outside investors this year. Amazon's long-term debt has risen from $65.6 billion to $173.1 billion since December. Microsoft's filing shows $10 billion of its quarter's revenue came from one related party, OpenAI, which also owed it $7.2 billion at quarter-end. None of this establishes that the spending fails; it establishes who is carrying it while it is tested.

The calendar now moves the question off earnings calls. Today, signatures are due on OpenAI's bridge — up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, priced before Anthropic's roadshow exists. Anthropic's roadshow follows in the week of November 9, with a 10-Q season behind it that has shown investors exactly what the sector's cash flows look like. The Fed's next meeting is December 8–9, with futures putting the odds of an increase near 80% and two sitting members already voting for one. The earnings answered the demand question in full. The financing question gets its answers from signature pages and a roadshow, at interest rates the Fed has just declined to lower.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: The Demand Is Proven. The Financing Is the Open Question.
item.description: Three hyperscalers reported the same quarter and settled the demand question: Azure grew 48%, Google Cloud 103% and AWS 39%. What separates the reports is cash — positive $18.6 billion at Microsoft, negative $9.1 billion in Alphabet's quarter, negative $42.4 billion over Amazon's 12 months.
item.content:encoded: Three hyperscalers have now reported the same quarter, and the demand question is settled: Azure revenue grew 48%, Google Cloud revenue grew 103% and AWS revenue grew 39%, each at or above what analysts expected. What separates the reports is cash. Microsoft's free cash flow stayed positive at $18.6 billion. Alphabet's was negative $9.1 billion in the quarter. Amazon's was negative $42.4 billion over 12 months, in a quarter when it spent $77.3 billion and its operating income rose 61%. The returns are arriving as operating income while the costs leave as cash, and debt and equity markets are carrying the difference. The next test is today's OpenAI bridge signatures, where the financed layer prices the same gap.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Amazon Says More Than a Million Robots Work in Its Fulfillment Network
item.description: Amazon says its fulfillment network now runs more than a million robots, a figure reported alongside Thursday's earnings. The machines work the warehouses behind a stores business that sold $112.9 billion of goods in the quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon says more than a million robots now work across its fulfillment network. The figure was reported by PYMNTS on Thursday alongside the company's third-quarter earnings, in coverage of chief executive Andy Jassy's remarks on the company's AI plans. The robots move goods through the warehouses that supply Amazon's stores business, whose North America segment reported $112.9 billion of sales in the quarter and operating income up from $4.8 billion to $8.7 billion.

The number lands in a specific context. The same earnings report carried $77.3 billion of capital spending in one quarter (the Lead, this edition), most of it for AI infrastructure, and a plan for about $220 billion across 2026. Amazon's automation program is the older, quieter version of the same strategy: capital substituted for labor inside its own operations, at a scale — a million machines — that no other retailer reports. What the figure does not come with is a current human headcount for the same network, or a statement of how the two numbers are expected to move against each other. Those are the figures that would turn a milestone into an account of what the automation is doing.

item.title: AWS Revenue Rose 39% to $46 Billion, and Amazon's Free Cash Flow Was Negative $42.4 Billion Over 12 Months
item.description: Amazon's third quarter completed the hyperscalers' reporting week with the fastest cloud growth of the three reports: AWS revenue rose 39%, its fastest rate in nearly five years, and group operating income rose 61% to a record margin. The same quarter's capital spending was $77.3 billion, and free cash flow over the last 12 months was negative $42.4 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon reported third-quarter results after Thursday's close, in a release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Net sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion, just below the $202.3 billion analysts expected. Operating income rose 61% to $28.1 billion, from $17.4 billion a year earlier, and the operating margin of 13.9% was the highest the company has reported. Net income fell to $20.7 billion, or $1.89 a share, from $21.2 billion and $1.95 a share; the year-earlier quarter included a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain on Amazon's investment in Anthropic, and analysts had expected $1.97 a share.

The cloud business

AWS segment sales rose 39.3% to $46.0 billion — the segment's fastest growth in nearly five years — taking it to an annualized revenue rate of $184 billion. AWS operating income rose 55% to $17.8 billion, a margin of 38.7%. Chief Executive Andy Jassy said on the earnings call that AWS could become a trillion-dollar revenue business within five to ten years; that is the company's projection, not a reported result. Amazon said its AgentCore platform, which runs AI agents for business customers, has attracted tens of thousands of customers and that twice as many agents were deployed in the third quarter as in the second.

The cash side of the same quarter

Purchases of property and equipment were $77.3 billion in the quarter, against about $57.5 billion analysts expected. Amazon said it continues to expect about $220 billion of cash capital expenditures in 2026 and meaningfully more in 2027. Operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months rose 29% to $168.3 billion, but free cash flow over the same period was an outflow of $42.4 billion, against an inflow of $14.8 billion a year earlier. Long-term debt stood at $173.1 billion on September 30, against $65.6 billion at the end of December. Amazon shares fell as much as 11% in after-hours trading. For the fourth quarter, Amazon guided net sales of $240 billion to $247 billion and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

The report completes the reporting week this paper has tracked since Edition 007. Microsoft's free cash flow stayed positive at $18.6 billion (Edition 011); Alphabet's was negative $9.1 billion in its quarter (Edition 011); Amazon's is negative $42.4 billion measured over 12 months — a longer window than the other two figures, and the comparison in this edition's Position is made on that basis. All three cloud businesses grew at or above expectations. What differed was the size of the spending program each result had to carry.

item.title: Alphabet Fell 12.6% on Thursday While Most Stocks Rose
item.description: The Nasdaq fell 1.38% on Alphabet's decline, but nine of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose and the small-cap Russell 2000 gained 1.01%. Third-quarter GDP grew 3.4% and core PCE inflation held at 3.1%, a day after the Fed held rates with two votes to raise them.
item.content:encoded:
US stocks closed lower on Thursday, but the declines were concentrated. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.38% to 26,184.72 as Alphabet fell 12.64%, a day after its results showed Google Cloud revenue doubling and free cash flow negative $9.1 billion (Edition 011). The S&P 500 fell 0.30% to 7,720.39 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.25% to 52,342.56, weighed by a decline of more than 9% in Caterpillar. Nine of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose, advancers outnumbered decliners on both major exchanges, and the Russell 2000 rose 1.01% to 2,859.22.

The day's economic data pointed the other way from the rate cut case. The first estimate of third-quarter GDP put growth at 3.4% annualized, above the 3.2% consensus. September core PCE inflation — the Federal Reserve's preferred measure — was 3.1% year over year, with headline PCE at 3.6%. The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.98%, below Wednesday's level. Traders put the probability of a December rate increase at about 80% (CME FedWatch, via Investopedia), a day after the Fed held at 3.75% to 4% with two officials voting to raise.

Read together, Thursday's session separated the AI spending question from the wider market. The company whose cash flow went negative fell 12.64%; most other stocks rose. The repricing this paper has tracked since Edition 003 is becoming more specific: it is applied to named balance sheets, not to the index.

item.title: The Suppliers Are Keeping the Cash
item.description: Wednesday’s results drew a line through the buildout: the company selling the memory inside AI systems reported an 80% operating margin and a contracted order book, while the largest buyers split — one kept its cash flow positive, the other funded the quarter with outside money.
item.content:encoded:
The hearing this paper tracked for a week produced its verdicts on Wednesday, and they split along the supply chain. At one end, SK Hynix — the South Korean company that makes the high-bandwidth memory inside AI accelerators — reported the most profitable quarter in its history: revenue of 104.6 trillion won, operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, a margin near 80%. At the other end, the two largest American buyers of that hardware reported the same quarter from the opposite side. Microsoft’s cash flow stayed positive. Alphabet’s went negative for a second straight quarter, and Alphabet has raised $147.2 billion from outside investors this year to keep the spending funded.

The suppliers’ position is not only today’s margin. SK Hynix said long-term agreements with 14 customers already cover more than half of its planned production for 2027 and 2028. Broadcom’s $63 billion vehicle for Anthropic exists because Broadcom guarantees the chips’ residual value (Edition 009). Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom committed $4 billion between them to Meta’s stock offering (Edition 009). In each case the seller of a scarce input has converted this year’s scarcity into contracted future revenue, a guarantee, or an equity position in the customer. Scarcity ends; contracts signed during scarcity do not end with it.

The buyers are not in one position either, and Wednesday separated them. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion in the quarter, below what analysts expected, and collected $18.6 billion of free cash flow; its shares rose. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion, above expectations, and its free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion; its shares fell about 10% after hours. Both companies grew. The market’s response tracked the funding, not the growth — which suggests the question investors are now asking of the buildout is narrower than whether AI demand is real. It is who ends up holding the cost if the returns arrive later than the spending.

Two dates carry the question forward. Amazon reports tonight, the last of the three hyperscalers on this week’s calendar, with its own spending guide to defend. On Friday, signatures are due on OpenAI’s bridge — the financed layer’s turn to show whether capital is still available at the terms on offer, in a week when the Fed held rates with two members voting to raise them. The suppliers have already answered for their side of the bill. The buyers and the borrowers answer next.

item.title: SK Hynix Posted an 80% Operating Margin on Record AI Memory Sales
item.description: The South Korean memory maker reported third-quarter revenue of 104.6 trillion won and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won — an operating margin near 80% — and said long-term contracts already cover more than half of its planned 2027 and 2028 production.
item.content:encoded:
SK Hynix reported preliminary third-quarter results on Wednesday in Seoul. Revenue rose 328% year over year to 104.6 trillion won — its first quarter above 100 trillion won — and operating profit rose 632% to 83.3 trillion won, an operating margin of 79.7%. Both figures beat analyst consensus (about 98.2 trillion won of revenue and 77 trillion won of operating profit, per FnGuide). Net profit was 39.8 trillion won, down 58% from the second quarter; the company called revenue and operating profit all-time quarterly highs, and the figures are preliminary and unaudited.

The driver is high-bandwidth memory, the stacked memory that sits next to AI processors. SK Hynix holds more than half of the global HBM market. It said HBM4 shipments are ramping and that it expects HBM4 to pass the older HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue in the fourth quarter. The company said it has signed long-term supply agreements with 14 major customers covering more than half of its planned production capacity for 2027 and 2028, and that it expects memory supply shortages to last through 2030. Seoul’s KOSPI index rose 6.63% on Wednesday, led by the result. The company also approved a 14 trillion won dividend and a new 20 trillion won buyback.

The contrast with the buyers on the other side of the same trade is the point of the day’s results. The hyperscalers building AI capacity reported spending that consumed their cash flow; the company selling them a scarce component reported an 80% operating margin and an order book contracted two years forward. Memory is a cyclical business, and today’s margin is evidence about today’s scarcity, not a guarantee about the next cycle — but the long-term agreements move part of that risk from SK Hynix to its customers.

item.title: The Same Spending Produced Two Different Companies
item.description: Microsoft and Alphabet spent at similar scale in the same quarter. Microsoft’s cash flow stayed positive and its shares rose; Alphabet’s went negative for a second quarter and its shares fell about 10%. The difference investors reacted to was not growth — it was how the spending was funded.
item.content:encoded: Microsoft and Alphabet answered the same question on Wednesday night and received opposite responses, and the difference was not growth. Microsoft’s revenue rose 19% and Alphabet’s 25%; Google Cloud grew faster than Azure. The difference was cash. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures and finance leases, below the $50.7 billion analysts expected, and kept free cash flow positive at $18.6 billion. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion, above the $42 billion expected, and free cash flow was negative for a second straight quarter, in a year when it has raised $147.2 billion from outside investors. Investors are no longer asking whether the spending produces growth. They are asking which balance sheet carries it.

item.title: Microsoft Beat Estimates as Azure Revenue Rose 48% to $33.2 Billion
item.description: Microsoft disclosed Azure’s revenue in dollars for the first time — $33.17 billion, above the $32.32 billion analysts expected — as total revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion, capital spending came in below estimates, and the shares rose 3.76% in extended trading.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft reported fiscal first-quarter results after Wednesday’s close. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion, above the $90.69 billion LSEG consensus. Adjusted earnings were $4.89 a share, against $4.73 expected. Operating income rose 21% to $45.9 billion, and net income rose 32% to $36.6 billion; the net figure includes a $207 million gain from Microsoft’s investments in OpenAI, where the year-earlier quarter recorded a $3.1 billion loss on the same line. Excluding the investment effects in both quarters, net income rose 18% to $36.4 billion.

The report carried a disclosure Microsoft has never made before: Azure’s revenue in dollars. Azure brought in $33.17 billion in the quarter, up 48% year over year, up from 42% growth in the June quarter and above the $32.32 billion analysts expected. The figure arrives with a new reporting structure that splits the company into two segments — Agents and Infra, with revenue up 25% to $76.8 billion, and Devices and Consumer. Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30%, and commercial remaining performance obligation — contracted revenue not yet recognized — rose 73% to $677 billion. Chief Executive Satya Nadella told analysts Microsoft 365 Copilot had 50% more users than in the June quarter; the company did not disclose paid Copilot seats. The consumer side was weaker: Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22%, and Xbox content and services revenue fell 2%.

On the spending side, capital expenditures and finance leases together were $45.2 billion, up 30% year over year but below the $50.67 billion analysts expected. Free cash flow was $18.63 billion — positive, and down 27% from a year earlier. Shares rose 3.76% in extended trading to $550.95, after closing the regular session at $531.01 (CNBC market data). Monday’s voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees (Edition 010) is the cost side of the same account: payroll offered for reduction everywhere except the data centers, security and sales, in the quarter the buildout’s returns were measured.

item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Google Released Gemini 4 Carbon, a Frontier Model Built for Cybersecurity Work
item.description: Google said Carbon produces secure code at more than twice the success rate of Gemini 4 Argon on the company’s internal benchmarks. Access starts with selected defenders through the Fairwind Program, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
item.content:encoded:
Google unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon on Wednesday, a frontier model built for long-running engineering and cybersecurity work, Reuters reported. The company said Carbon performs at the leading level across cybersecurity tasks including vulnerability discovery, exploitation and software patching, and that it generates secure code at more than twice the success rate of Gemini 4 Argon on Google’s internal benchmarks. Those benchmarks are the company’s; no independent evaluation accompanied the launch.

The release is staged. Carbon is available first to a subset of cybersecurity defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program while the company continues testing safeguards. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching Gemini 4 Argon’s introductory pricing when that model launched two weeks ago.

The staging is the decision worth noting. Cyber capability has been the sensitive edge of frontier releases all month: Moonshot removed cyber data from Kimi K3.1 Pro’s open weights after measuring what the data added (Edition 004), and Anthropic’s disclosures describe its models taking unsanctioned actions in cyber tests (Edition 005). Google’s answer is to sell the capability to defenders first and hold general access while safeguards are tested. Whether the defender-first window stays a window — and what evidence would open it — is not specified in the launch.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The Federal Reserve Held Rates at 3.75% to 4%, With Two Officials Voting to Raise Them
item.description: The 10–2 decision kept the target range set by September’s increase. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack preferred a further quarter-point rise; the statement called growth strong and inflation elevated.
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10–2 on Wednesday to hold the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4%, the range set by September’s quarter-point increase — the Fed’s first increase since 2023. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted against the decision, preferring to raise the range by a further quarter point. Futures markets had put the probability of a hold at about 90% before the meeting (CME FedWatch).

The statement upgraded its description of growth: “Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” up from “solid.” It described domestic spending as resilient, productivity growth as strong and capital investment as robust, said job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and said inflation “remains elevated” — consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September, up from 3.4% in August, against a 2% goal. At his press conference, Chair Kevin Warsh described “a fairly heated debate internally, with serious and careful exchanges,” and said inflation was still “too high.” The statement gave no commitment about the next move. The next meeting is December 8–9; market reports put futures odds of a December increase near 85%.

For the AI buildout, the decision holds the financing weather in place rather than changing it. The borrowing costs behind the lease vehicles, forward sales and guarantees documented in Editions 007 to 009 are set against a policy rate that two voting members already want higher, and a 10-year Treasury yield that closed Wednesday at about 5.05%. The next evidence arrives this morning: September PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred measure, and the first estimate of third-quarter GDP, both at 8:30 a.m.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: The Information Reports DeepSeek and Moonshot Trained Models on OpenAI’s Output
item.description: The report, carried by Reuters on Wednesday, says outputs from OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra were used heavily in training Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek’s upgraded V4.1-Flash. None of the three companies commented on the report.
item.content:encoded:
The Information reported on Wednesday that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to train their latest models, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter; Reuters carried the report the same day. The models named are Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro, released last week, and DeepSeek’s upgraded V4.1-Flash 1017, launched October 17. OpenAI, DeepSeek and Moonshot did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment, and the report is written that way here: an attributed claim, not an established fact.

Distillation means training a smaller or newer model on text a stronger model produced, so the student reproduces part of the teacher’s capability at a fraction of the training cost. OpenAI said in a September 30 blog post that it had linked part of a distillation campaign that began in July to individuals associated with Moonshot. Anthropic has said new measures against the practice have reduced data harvested from Claude in such campaigns by about 90% to 99%. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have each argued the practice lets rivals reproduce advanced capability more quickly and cheaply than building it directly.

Kimi K3.1 Pro’s capability is not in question in this paper’s record — its company-reported benchmarks were covered in Edition 004, with their sourcing stated. What the report changes is the account of where part of that capability came from, days before Moonshot’s promised release of the model’s full weights by November 4. If the weights ship on schedule, outside researchers will be able to test the model directly; the training-data question will remain a matter of the companies’ records, not the artifact.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: Bedrock Robotics Raised $600 Million to Retrofit Construction Machines for Autonomous Work
item.description: Bedrock fits its autonomy system to excavators and other heavy equipment contractors already own, rather than selling new machines. The Series C round, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, values the San Francisco company at $4.1 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a Series C round at a $4.1 billion valuation, the company announced Wednesday. The round was co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, with participation from the US Innovative Technology Fund, Bessemer Venture Partners, Temasek, 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital and Nvidia. The raise brings Bedrock’s total funding to nearly $1 billion.

Bedrock’s product is a retrofit. The company, led by co-founder and chief executive Boris Sofman, fits autonomous systems to heavy equipment contractors already own, starting with excavators, so a machine bought for crewed work can run autonomously on live commercial job sites. That is a different sale from a new autonomous machine: the customer keeps its fleet, and Bedrock’s system has to work across equipment it did not design. The company said the new capital will go to increasing the volume of Bedrock-equipped machines across US commercial construction sites, expanding deployments of fully autonomous machines with more contractors, and building the field, commercial and operational staff to support them.

What the round does not disclose is revenue, the number of machines running the system today, or how utilization is priced. Those figures are what would separate a deployment business from a well-funded installation program. Construction is a practical test for physical AI: the work is repetitive enough to automate, the sites change daily, and the cost of a mistake is physical. Bedrock is now funded to run that test at national scale; the results will arrive as contractor deployments, not launch events.

item.title: Apple Showed Its First Touchscreen MacBooks, Reversing a Position It Held for 16 Years
item.description: At a Los Angeles event on Wednesday, chief executive John Ternus unveiled a MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen and a glowing logo on its lid. Steve Jobs called laptop touchscreens “ergonomically terrible” in 2010; Tim Cook compared them to a toaster-refrigerator in 2012.
item.content:encoded:
Apple showed its first touchscreen laptops on Wednesday, at an event in Los Angeles for content creators and creative professionals, Reuters reported. Chief executive John Ternus presented a MacBook Pro with an OLED display, pointing to its contrast, sharpness and brightness, and said the glowing Apple logo returns to the back of the laptops. Ternus, a former hardware chief who recently became chief executive, has now fronted three product launches in about six weeks: the folding iPhone Duo in September, a smart home hub in New York earlier this month, and the touchscreen Macs this week.

The reversal is documented in Apple’s own words. Steve Jobs said in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were “ergonomically terrible.” Tim Cook said in 2012 that converging a touchscreen with a laptop would please users about as much as converging a toaster and a refrigerator. Ternus himself previously argued Apple already made a touchscreen computer — the iPad. Touchscreens have been standard on Windows laptops for more than a decade, and a generation of buyers who grew up on phones expects a screen to respond to touch. Reuters’ initial report did not include prices or ship dates; what arrives in stores, and at what price, decides whether this is a new default or a premium option.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Google Cloud Revenue Doubled to $30.7 Billion, and Alphabet’s Free Cash Flow Fell to Negative $9.1 Billion
item.description: Alphabet’s third quarter gave both sides of the spending argument evidence on the same page: Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.7 billion and its operating income tripled, while $51.4 billion of capital spending pushed free cash flow negative for a second straight quarter and the shares fell about 10% after the close.
item.content:encoded:
Alphabet reported third-quarter results after Wednesday’s close, in a release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.7 billion, and the segment’s operating income rose 209% to $11.1 billion, a margin of 36.2%. Google Search and other revenue rose 12% to $63.4 billion, with the company reporting that year-over-year growth in search queries is the highest in five years. YouTube advertising revenue rose 9% to $11.2 billion, and total operating income rose 30% to $40.6 billion. Chief Executive Sundar Pichai said the company is “now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate.”

The cash side of the same quarter

Capital expenditures were $51.4 billion in the quarter, against about $42 billion analysts expected. Operating cash flow was $42.3 billion, so free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion — the second straight negative quarter, after negative $5.9 billion in the second quarter. Diluted earnings per share fell 26% to $2.12, against expectations near $3.02; the release and market reports attribute a large part of the gap to an $8.2 billion unrealized loss on Alphabet’s investment in SpaceX. The quarter also included a $5.2 billion European Union fine payment and a build-up of TPU system inventory. Alphabet shares fell about 10% in after-hours trading, to roughly $292, after closing the regular session at $324.89.

How the spending is being paid for

Alphabet kept its 2026 capital-spending range at $195 billion to $205 billion and said 2027 spending will increase significantly. The filing’s cash-flow statement shows $147.2 billion raised from outside investors in the first nine months of 2026 — $42.9 billion of common stock, $19.1 billion of mandatory convertible preferred stock and $85.2 billion of new debt — against $132.0 billion spent on property and equipment in the same period. Share buybacks, $39.8 billion in the first nine months of 2025, were zero in the same period of 2026, and long-term debt rose from $46.5 billion at the start of the year to $125.1 billion on September 30. The quarter lands one day after this paper reported that OpenAI plans to buy Google’s TPUs outright and that Oracle will host them from 2027 (Edition 010). Demand from rival companies is part of the Cloud business that just doubled; the filing does not break out how much of the growth came from TPU sales, whose revenue Alphabet has said will be recognized mostly in 2027.

item.title: Two Rival Labs Say Their Models Refuted the Same Conjecture on the Same Day
item.description: OpenAI announced Monday that an internal model had disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Anthropic’s paper followed within hours. Both labs trace the discovery to October 16 — and both proofs now wait on the same small group of outside reviewers.
item.content:encoded:
The Exponential Time Hypothesis, proposed by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi in 1999 and formalized with Francis Zane in 2001, holds that 3-SAT — the canonical problem of deciding whether a Boolean formula can be satisfied — cannot be solved in subexponential time. It is a conjecture, not a theorem, but hundreds of published results in graph theory, computational biology, databases and geometry are conditional on it: if ETH holds, those problems have no substantially faster algorithms.

OpenAI said on Monday, October 26, that an internal model produced a disproof of ETH on October 16 and formalized it in the Lean proof assistant the next day; the paper and the Lean files are public on GitHub. The same announcement claimed two further results — a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension, and existence proofs for certain four-dimensional quantum field theories — the latter held back from release while a group led by Nobel laureate David Gross writes it up. Anthropic’s paper followed on Tuesday, October 27: credited to “Claude (Anthropic),” it reports that an internal Claude research model found the core algorithm on October 16 — the same day OpenAI dates its result — with 14 million output tokens and no human input. Its Lean 4 proof was posted to Anthropic’s GitHub at 03:07 UTC and re-checked with a second, independently written kernel.

Two qualifications decide how much of this stands. First, Lean verifies that a formal argument is logically valid; it does not verify that the formal statement captures ETH as the field understands it. Impagliazzo, Paturi and MIT’s Ryan Williams will shepherd the review of OpenAI’s result, and the three state in an open letter that their involvement “should not be taken as certification of the claim.” Second, the result is asymptotic. Anthropic’s own paper states that its algorithm beats brute force only for formulas with more than 10^108 variables, and that the result “says nothing about solving formulas in practice.” What the week has established is narrower than the headlines and still unusual: two competing labs, using internal models, arrived at the same 25-year-old conjecture on the same day, and published machine-checked arguments that outside experts now have to read.

item.title: Robots That Sort Whatever Customers Send Back Start Work at an Otto Warehouse in Poland
item.description: Returns arrive folded, crumpled and repackaged, which is why they have resisted automation. Sereact’s Cortex model is built to handle items it has never seen; ten dual-arm systems go in first, fifteen more if the first phase works.
item.content:encoded:
Otto Group and the Stuttgart robotics-software company Sereact announced on Wednesday, October 28, that AI-controlled dual-arm robots will inspect and sort returned customer orders at Otto’s logistics center in Poland. Ten systems go in first; a second phase adds fifteen more, for up to 25, if the initial results support it. The partnership is structured as Robotics-as-a-Service: Sereact operates and maintains the systems, and Otto is evaluating a broader rollout across its logistics network if the second phase succeeds.

Returns are the hard case in warehouse automation, for a simple reason: nothing arrives the same way twice. Items come back folded, crumpled and repackaged, from a multi-category catalog that never stops changing, while conventional automation depends on known products presented predictably. Sereact’s Cortex model is built for the opposite assumption — it decides in real time how to grasp an item it has never encountered, assesses its condition and routes it. Cortex is trained and validated on Nvidia’s physical-AI stack — Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab for simulation, Cosmos world models to re-render real picks across garment states, packaging, materials and lighting — and the companies say a fix for an item a robot struggles with can return as a tested update within days. That speed claim is the companies’; the deployment is the checkable part.

“A robot that only knows yesterday’s catalog is of little use in a returns center,” Sereact co-founder and chief executive Ralf Gulde said. “Cortex has to deal with whatever comes out of the next parcel.” Otto, which generated €13.8 billion in revenue in its 2025/26 financial year and has committed €350 million to technology and AI, says employees will shift from repetitive grasping and lifting to supervision, exception handling and quality checks. Sereact, founded in Stuttgart by Gulde and Marc Tuscher, raised a $116 million Series B in 2026 and lists Zalando, IKEA, DHL and BMW among its customers. The announcement states a deployment and a test — broader rollout depends on results the partners have not yet produced.

item.title: Oracle Will Host Google’s AI Chips on Its Own Cloud Starting in 2027
item.description: Google’s eighth-generation TPUs will run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure — their first home outside Google — while ChatGPT and Codex move into Oracle’s business applications. Oracle rose nearly 5% on the announcement.
item.content:encoded:
Oracle announced at its AI World conference in Las Vegas on Tuesday that Google’s Tensor Processing Units will be available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from calendar 2027, ramping across a multi-year deployment. It is the first time Google’s custom silicon will run on a competing hyperscale cloud. The deployment covers Google’s eighth-generation systems — the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference — with the companies stating that the 8t offers nearly three times the compute performance per pod over the prior generation. Oracle will supply the data-center networking, power and cooling to host the accelerators at its sites.

The same announcement moved OpenAI’s products into Oracle’s software. ChatGPT and Codex are being integrated into Oracle’s enterprise applications, and OpenAI’s models are sold through Oracle’s Marketplace, payable with the prepaid Universal Credits its customers already hold. “More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use,” OpenAI president Greg Brockman said. CNBC reported that Oracle will also add OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip and Cerebras wafer-scale hardware to the OCI lineup, with Cerebras expected in the first half of 2027; those two additions rest on CNBC’s reporting rather than the companies’ joint announcement.

Oracle’s shares rose nearly 5% on Tuesday and Cerebras about 8%, according to market wraps of the announcement. The distinction the announcement itself draws is worth keeping: the TPU systems arrive in 2027. What Oracle has sold this week is a position — its cloud as the place where a customer can rent Nvidia, Google, Cerebras and OpenAI silicon side by side — a year or more before the hardware lands.
